usage: Can I get a menu, please
The single most useful sentence when you sit down; 좀 softens the request
What staff say while handing it over
에 marks the menu as the location where the item is absent
You see the menu by QR code
Many places now have no paper menu, just a QR sticker on the table
examples: 메뉴판 좀 주세요.
Please give me the menu.
The bare, can't-go-wrong version — learn this first
저기요, 메뉴판 좀 다시 주시겠어요?
Excuse me, could you bring the menu again?
주시겠어요 is the extra-polite re-request after you've already ordered drinks
메뉴판이 한국어밖에 없어서 사진 보고 시켰어요.
The menu was only in Korean, so I ordered by looking at the photos.
밖에 + negative = 'only'; a very common newcomer reality
nuance: 메뉴판 is the physical object — the booklet you hold or the board on the wall — built from 메뉴 ('menu') + 판 (板, 'board/plate'). The contrast that trips up English speakers is 메뉴 vs 메뉴판: 메뉴 is abstract (the offerings, or even a single dish, as in '오늘의 메뉴'), so if you say '메뉴 주세요' staff may think you're naming or asking about a dish, not requesting the booklet. When you want the thing physically brought to you, always say 메뉴판. The register is neutral and everyday; '메뉴판 주세요' (or the softer '메뉴판 좀 주세요') is perfectly polite in any restaurant, from a tiny diner to a nice one. It habitually pairs with 주세요 (give me), 보다 (look at), and 있다/없다 (it's on / not on the menu).

Pronouncing it as two separate words 'menu pan' — it is one compound noun, 메뉴판, said in one breath.
Adding 을/를 awkwardly in speech ('메뉴판을 주세요') — natural spoken Korean usually drops the object particle here: '메뉴판 주세요'.

usage: The staff's standard opening question (honorific 하시-)
Polite phrasing staff use when approaching the table
들어가다 ('go in') = the kitchen has received it
취소되다 (be cancelled); useful if you change your mind fast
examples: 주문할게요.
I'd like to order.
The simplest way to flag that you're ready
주문 아직 안 했어요. 조금만 더 볼게요.
We haven't ordered yet. We'll look a bit more.
Buys time when staff come too early; 아직 = 'not yet'
단체라서 주문이 한꺼번에 들어갔어요.
Since it's a big group, the order all went in at once.
한꺼번에 = 'all at once'; links naturally to 단체
nuance: 주문 is the noun 'order', from 注文 (注 'pour/note down' + 文 'writing') — originally 'to write down a request', which fits ordering perfectly. The verb is 주문하다, and a key contrast is 주문하다 vs 시키다: both mean 'to order', but 시키다 is more casual and also means 'to make someone do something', so toward staff the cleaner, slightly more standard choice is 주문하다 (시키다 is fine among friends: '뭐 시킬까?'). Knowing the bare noun unlocks the phrases you hear constantly — '주문 도와드릴게요', '주문 들어갔어요', '주문 확인해 주세요' — where 주문 stands alone. Register is neutral and identical in casual and formal dining. It collocates with 하다, 들어가다 (go in), 받다 (take an order), 확인하다 (confirm), and 취소하다 (cancel).

mistakes: Confusing 주문 (an order) with 주말 (weekend) — they look similar to beginners but are unrelated; mis-saying one for the other changes the meaning entirely.
Defaulting to 시키다 with staff ('이거 시켜 주세요') — understandable but a touch blunt; '이거 주문할게요' or simply '이거 주세요' sounds cleaner to servers.
Treating 주문 as a verb on its own ('주문 주세요') — you need 주문하다, e.g. '주문할게요', or attach 하다.

english: an extra order / addition (more of something)
usage: An extra bowl of rice, please
'추가요' alone is a complete spoken request
추가되다 = 'be addable'; 사리 = extra noodle bundle
추가 + 주문하다 when calling staff for a second round
추가 요금 = surcharge; checks if the add-on costs more
examples: 공깃밥 추가요.
An extra bowl of rice, please.
Minimal pattern: '[item] 추가요' gets you more and gets it rung up
고기 다 먹어서 2인분 추가했어요.
We finished the meat, so we added two more portions.
추가하다 as a verb; classic Korean BBQ move
라면에 치즈 추가하면 천 원이에요.
Adding cheese to the ramen is 1,000 won.
에 marks what you add the topping to; shows add-ons can cost money
nuance: 추가 is 追加 (追 'chase/pursue' + 加 'add') — literally 'to add on in pursuit', i.e. an additional order: more rice, more meat, an extra topping, a second drink. The sharp contrast is 추가 vs 리필: 추가 means ordering more and usually paying for it, whereas 리필 ('refill') implies a free top-up of the same item. So for paid extras say 추가, for free soda/coffee/side-dish top-ups say 리필. Attaching -요 ('추가요') turns the bare noun into a full, polite spoken request, which is how locals add items without a whole sentence. Register is casual-but-polite and works everywhere; the verb is 추가하다. It pairs with 주문 (order more), 요금 (extra charge), 사리/공깃밥 (extra noodles/rice), and 인분 (extra portions).

mistakes: Saying '더 주세요' for paid add-ons — fine for free 반찬, but for chargeable items say '[X] 추가요' so staff actually ring it up instead of just topping you off.
Assuming 추가 is always free — unlike 리필, an 추가 normally costs money; confirm with '추가 요금 있어요?' first.
Using bare 추가 as a verb ('밥 추가 주세요') is understandable but the cleaner forms are '밥 추가요' or '밥 추가해 주세요'.

usage: The key question — really asks 'is it free?'
되나요 is slightly softer and very natural
무한(無限) = 'limitless'; common at salad bars and buffets
리필하다 + 드릴까요 — what staff sometimes offer you
examples: 리필 돼요?
Can I get a refill?
The one phrase to memorize before assuming top-ups are free
여기 콜라 리필 돼요?
Can I refill the cola here?
여기 ('here') checks this specific place's policy
커피 리필은 한 번만 무료예요.
The coffee refill is free only once.
한 번만 = 'just once'; shows refills can be limited even when offered
nuance: 리필 is a loanword from English 'refill', and it specifically carries the nuance of getting more of the same item for free — drinks, side dishes, coffee, popcorn. The dividing line from its cousin 추가 is exactly cost: 리필 = same thing, no charge; 추가 = more (often a different/larger amount) that you pay for. So '콜라 리필 돼요?' asks whether free refills exist, while '콜라 추가요' means 'add another (paid) cola'. Don't assume 됨; the verb 되다 here means 'is it allowed/available', so '리필 돼요?' literally checks the policy before you walk up to the machine. Register is casual and everyday. The verb is 리필하다, and it collocates with 무한(unlimited), 무료(free), 음료/커피(drink/coffee), and 한 번만(only once).

Treating 되다 as 'become' here — in '리필 돼요?' it means 'is it possible/allowed', not 'does it become a refill'.

english: pager / buzzer (that vibrates when food is ready)
usage: Come when the buzzer goes off
가져가다 = 'take (it) along' as staff hand it over
반납하다(返納) = 'return'; expected after you pick up food
Where do I get the buzzer?
어디서 = 'where (at)'; useful in busy self-order places
examples: 진동벨 울리면 오세요.
Come when the buzzer rings.
The core instruction you must understand at the counter
진동벨 울려서 음식 가지러 갔어요.
The buzzer went off, so I went to get the food.
-(으)러 가다 = 'go in order to'; the self-pickup flow
진동벨 진동이랑 불빛이 같이 와요.
The buzzer vibrates and lights up together.
이랑 = casual 'and'; describes how it signals
nuance: 진동벨 literally stitches together 진동 (振動, 'vibration') + 벨 ('bell'), so 'vibration bell' — the pager you're handed at counter-service spots, food courts, and many cafes. Unlike a plain 벨 (a doorbell or a call button you press), the 진동벨 is the thing that buzzes you, signaling that you go fetch the food yourself. Recognizing the word is what matters most: staff will say '진동벨 울리면 오세요' and fully expect you to walk up, not wait to be served. After pickup, you 반납 (return) it. Register is neutral and everyday. It collocates with 울리다 (ring/buzz), 가져가다 (take along), 반납하다 (return), and 받다 (receive one).

usage: 은 marks water as the topic; extremely common sign/phrase
Where you grab water, side dishes, utensils
셀프바 = self-serve bar; staff pointing you to the station
examples: 물은 셀프예요.
Water is self-serve.
The four-syllable sentence that means 'go get it yourself'
물이랑 단무지는 셀프라서 저쪽에서 가져오세요.
Water and pickled radish are self-serve, so get them over there.
셀프라서 = 'because it's self-serve'; classic instruction
여기 셀프라서 수저도 직접 챙겨야 해요.
It's self-serve here, so you grab your own utensils too.
직접 = 'in person/yourself'; sets the expectation for newcomers
nuance: 셀프 is the English 'self' borrowed as a noun/adjective, and in eateries it is shorthand for 셀프서비스 — it tells you no one will bring it: water, utensils (수저), side dishes (반찬), or refills are yours to fetch. The natural opposite is having staff bring things, and a near phrase is 직접 ('in person, yourself'), which often appears alongside it ('직접 가져오세요'). When you see '셀프' on a sign or hear '물은 셀프예요', the cue is to stand up and go get it from the dispenser or 셀프 코너. Register is casual and everyday, and the word is ubiquitous in Korean restaurants. It collocates with 물(water), 반찬(side dishes), 코너/바(station/bar), and the verbs 가져오다(bring) and 챙기다(grab/take).

Reading 셀프 as a brand or product name — here it simply means 'self-service'.
Forgetting that 셀프 often extends to utensils and refills, not just water — at a '셀프' spot you grab your own 수저 too.

usage: Make it a large (double) portion, please
로 marks 곱빼기 as the form/manner you want it in
How much is the large portion?
examples: 짜장면 곱빼기로 주세요.
Jjajangmyeon, the large portion, please.
The textbook way to upsize a noodle dish
배고파서 짬뽕 곱빼기로 시켰어요.
I was starving, so I ordered the large jjamppong.
-아서 gives the reason; very natural at a Chinese-Korean spot
곱빼기 시켰는데도 부족했어요.
Even though I got the large, it wasn't enough.
-는데도 = 'even though'; casual exaggeration about appetite
nuance: 곱빼기 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean) from 곱 ('multiplied, double') + the suffix -빼기, so it means roughly a double serving. Crucially it is tied to noodle and rice-bowl dishes — 짜장면, 짬뽕, 볶음밥 — and is the local way to get more food for a small surcharge: '[dish] 곱빼기로 주세요'. The contrast learners need is 곱빼기 vs 추가/2인분: 곱빼기 makes the single bowl bigger, while 추가 or 2인분 means ordering an additional separate serving (used for meat, side items, etc.). It does not apply to soups, BBQ meat, or drinks. Register is casual, and you'll mainly hear it at 중국집 (Chinese-Korean restaurants) and noodle houses. It collocates with -로 주세요, 시키다 (order), 얼마예요 (how much), and dish names like 짜장면/짬뽕.

usage: 로 marks the set as the option you choose
The set is cheaper than à la carte
examples: 세트로 주세요.
I'll have the set, please.
The default upgrade line at fast food
햄버거 단품 말고 세트로 할게요.
I'll get the burger as a combo, not just the burger alone.
말고 = 'not (this) but'; the 단품 vs 세트 choice in one sentence
세트로 시키면 음료랑 감자튀김이 같이 나와요.
If you order the set, a drink and fries come together.
-(으)면 = 'if'; explains what a 세트 includes
nuance: 세트 is the English 'set' borrowed to mean a combo — a main plus a drink and/or sides at one bundled price. Its direct opposite, and the contrast you must know, is 단품 (單品, 'single item', i.e. à la carte): '세트로 주세요' bundles everything, '단품으로 주세요' gets just the main. Don't confuse 세트 with 사이드 either — 세트 is the whole bundle, 사이드 is one side item inside or beside it. Asking for '세트로 주세요' is the default at fast food and many casual spots, and the price gap with 단품 is the usual reason people choose it. Register is neutral and everyday. It collocates with -로 (해 주세요/할게요), 단품 (à la carte), 메뉴 (combo menu), and numbered orders like 1번 세트.

mistakes: Assuming the displayed price is the 세트 price — menus often show the 단품 (single-item) price; ask '세트로 얼마예요?'.
Confusing 세트 (the whole combo) with 사이드 (the individual side item) — a 세트 contains sides, but 사이드 alone is just one add-on.
Saying '세트 주세요' without specifying which — at a counter, name it: '불고기버거 세트로 주세요' or '1번 세트요'.

english: a side dish / side item (menu add-on)
usage: What side items do you have?
뭐 있어요 = 'what is there'; asks what add-ons are offered
I'll have fries as a side
로 marks fries as the chosen side
추가하다 ties 사이드 to a paid add-on
The main and a side together
examples: 사이드 메뉴 뭐 있어요?
What sides do you have?
Opens the conversation about add-ons
치킨 시키면서 사이드로 치즈볼 추가했어요.
While ordering chicken, I added cheese balls as a side.
-(으)면서 = 'while'; the classic 치킨 delivery move
피자 사이드로 콜라랑 윙 시켰어요.
For pizza sides I ordered cola and wings.
사이드로 = 'as a side'; typical delivery combo
nuance: 사이드 is the English 'side', meaning the optional side items on a menu — fries, wings, cheese balls, garlic bread — and the contrast that matters is 사이드 vs 반찬: 사이드 is a paid, ordered add-on (especially at chicken, pizza, and burger places), whereas 반찬 is the free Korean side dishes that come automatically with a meal. So fries you 'order as a 사이드'; kimchi and pickled radish are 반찬 and arrive at no charge. You'll see a labeled '사이드 메뉴' section, heavily used in 배달 (delivery) ordering. The natural pairing is 사이드로 + dish + 주세요/시키다 ('as a side, give me / I'll order'). Register is casual. It collocates with 메뉴 (side menu), -로 (as a side), 추가하다 (add), and 메인 (the main).

usage: Can I make a group reservation?
